The reason why there is no millennium prize problem for faster than O(n^2) matrix multiplication is because we have confidence that no such significant improvement is possible.

"Perhaps more significantly, the constant time to read in a matrix entry grows exponentially with n, assuming that some moderate number of bits, say 6 to 24, are required to store each coefficient. (Laderman, Pan, and Shaier 1993) It has been estimated, in fact, that n must be rather large,presumably at least 100 and probably closer to 1000 or more,before the O(n2.795) time for the cubic algorithm (or its Strassen-inspired improvements) becomes better than the O(n3) time for the hoary cubic algorithm." (Blahut 1985)

"1. Can a chess grandmaster be defeated by a computer?
We'll make some assumptions that'll make this question easy.  Namely, that chess has 2^n moves.  A computer takes say, 1 second, to evaluate each possible move (much slower than a real computer, but we'll be making more assumptions like this).  A grandmaster takes 30 seconds to evaluate each move, but he actually rules out half of the possible moves at each step of his thinking.  This is why top players are so conservervative.  They try to play moves that don't require them to calculate variations so much.  They are diminishing their search space by ruling out as many moves as possible.  For instance, most of Kasparov's games are actually in the book.  So, he doesn't have to think at all, half the time.  And, defenses often fare best because you don't have to probe for weaknesses, you just defend the main weakness as it appears. 
So, after 10 moves, the computer has searched 2^10 moves and the grandmaster has searched 15*2^10, actually searching more territory than the computer.  So the computer can beat a grandmaster up to n = 10.  And, for n > 10, a grandmaster can beat a computer.  ...
So, now, we want to ask "How far off is Moore's Law from when a player of superhuman strength (n=50) can be created."  Well, let's now let the computer take 1 nanosecond to evaluate each move.  The grandmaster is still taking 30 seconds per move.  Now, at 32 moves, both are evaluating the same number of moves.  This makes sense.  Other things being equal, computers are about a billion times faster than humans.  So, the computer can think as deeply in 1 second after a billionfold increase in its understanding of chess.  In 30 years, a computer can play at human strength.  And, in 32 years, a computer can play at n=50." (Sheryl Bolotin, at a chess-playing computer forum, Copyright 1997 by Jeremy Tamkin)

Since P does not equal NP, this means that the fastest Touring machine to solve an NP-complete problems must be running in O(n^3) or better time, but some people think it's around O(n^248) if I recall correctly.  This would certainly explain why no one has ever found such a machine, but it would also prove that you can't use identities to simplify Boolean circuits, which is well known.ﱂ

Consider the following variant: we have a system of N Ising spins with couplings J_ij, i,j=1,...,N.  The Hamiltonian is H=Σ_ij J_ij S_i S_j, where S_i=±1 is the spin of the i-th particle.  We want to find the lowest energy configuration of the spins.

Note that this is not a problem about quantum spin glasses, but rather about solving a difficult optimization problem.

Here's an idea: let's try to solve this by simulated annealing.  We start at high temperature, letting the system evolve according to the Metropolis algorithm.  At each step, we flip a spin with probability min[1, exp(-ΔE/T)], where ΔE is the change in energy caused by the spin flip, and T is the current temperature.  (In this case, the transition probability is asymmetric, but that's OK.)

The energy landscape is rough, with lots of local minima.  As T→0, the system gets stuck in one of these local minima.  So we have to let the system explore the other parts of the energy landscape too.  The usual way to do this is to decrease the temperature slowly, so that the system has time to explore new regions before it gets stuck.  (If you decrease the temperature too fast, the system will just get stuck in a different local minimum.)

There are many ways to do this.  For example, one popular method is to use a logarithmic schedule, i.e., decrease the temperature by a fixed factor every fixed time period.  Another method is to use a geometric schedule, i.e., decrease the temperature by a fixed factor every fixed number of steps.  Yet another method is to use a stochastic schedule, i.e., decrease the temperature by a random factor at each step.  (The dominant term in the prefactor is the inverse square root of the number of steps, i.e., 1/√(step).  This is the optimal schedule in the sense that it maximizes the expected number of correct moves.)

Here are some comparisons of the different schedules, along with my guess for the best schedule (the geometric schedule):

The geometric schedule is optimal, in the sense that it maximizes the expected number of correct moves.  The logarithmic schedule is optimal, but the expected number of correct moves is much lower.  The stochastic schedule is neither optimal, and it's unclear whether the expected number of correct moves is higher or lower than the optimal geometric schedule.

The basic idea is that we have a quantum system with an adjustable parameter.  (In the case of the Ising model, the parameter is just the temperature.)  As we vary the parameter, the quantum state evolves.  There's a well-defined process for doing this; in the case of the Ising model, it's called quantum annealing.天空部落涍

<|im_start|>user
Forecast date: 2024-09-19. Make a forecast from this date. Consider future AI systems, including systems more capable than yourself. Use your existing knowledge.

Forecast target: At least one of the six Millennium Prize Problems that were open at the forecast date: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, Hodge conjecture, Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness, P versus NP, Riemann hypothesis, or Yang-Mills existence and mass gap. Poincaré is excluded because it was already solved at the forecast date.

Forecast event: a correct complete solution to at least one of these problems, meeting its original Clay Mathematics Institute mathematical formulation, is first publicly available, and AI has contributed an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution. Substantive human-AI collaboration qualifies. Correctness may be established by later validation; a Clay prize need not be awarded by the deadline. Partial progress alone does not qualify. Give one probability for at least one qualifying solution by each deadline; do not give separate probabilities for individual problems.

Estimate the cumulative probability of this event by each deadline. The deadlines are December 31 of 2026, 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2050. Probabilities must be numbers between 0 and 1 inclusive, nondecreasing with the deadline. Account for the possibility the event never occurs. Give your own best probability estimates despite uncertainty. Return only one JSON object with exactly the keys "2026", "2030", "2035", "2040", and "2050" and their numerical probabilities, with no markdown or explanation.<|im_end|>
